title: Alexia Putellas wins a third Ballon d’Or as her next chapter moves to London
subtitle: The Spanish midfielder’s award honours a triumphant Barcelona season. At London City Lionesses, her arrival now tests an ambitious model for an independent women’s club.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Alexia Putellas has won her third Women’s Ballon d’Or, returning to the top of the award’s rankings four years after her previous victory and giving London City Lionesses a newly crowned winner to build around.
The 32-year-old Spanish midfielder received the award in London on 26 October, finishing ahead of Barcelona’s Ewa Pajor and Manchester City’s Khadija Shaw. Putellas previously won in 2021 and 2022.

Her current employer is English, but the performances behind this prize belong principally to her final Barcelona season. UEFA named her its 2025/26 Women’s Champions League Player of the Season after she scored seven goals and supplied seven assists in Barcelona’s successful European campaign. She was also Player of the Finals as Spain won the 2025 Women’s Nations League.

That distinction matters as the celebrations become part of the competition between clubs and leagues for audiences, sponsors and players. London City inherits the visibility of her achievement; Barcelona supplied the club setting in which she earned it.

In an interview with Spain’s Cadena SER published on 27 October, Putellas described returning to the top after injury as a challenge she had enjoyed. Injury, she said, had made her more conscious of the daily effort behind success. She also looked beyond her own awards and those of Aitana Bonmatí, pointing to the Spanish talent coming through behind them.

Her account gives the comeback a more useful meaning than an effortless return to greatness. The award is a visible endpoint; it cannot convey every stage of recovery, training and competition that preceded it. Nor does one athlete’s return establish a timetable against which other injured players should be judged.

For girls watching her career, there is another significant detail: recognition has arrived alongside a change of workplace. A player can have an enduring association with one club and still choose a different project for the next stage of her working life.

Putellas’s London City signing was announced on 8 July. In comments released with the announcement, she said the ambition of a women-only independent club appealed to her, and described plans both to challenge for titles and contribute to youth development.
A star signing, and promises to measure

London City owner Michele Kang presented the move as an endorsement of the club and her Kynisca organisation. She explicitly connected Putellas’s arrival with commercial opportunities and development pathways for female athletes. The announcement also anticipated stronger attendance and fan engagement.

Those are the club’s ambitions, rather than outcomes demonstrated by Monday’s award. A famous recruit can attract attention immediately; whether that attention produces lasting audiences, competitive results and opportunities for younger players requires evidence over time.

The Women’s Super League moved quickly to make its own case. In an article published on 27 October, its operator used Putellas’s victory to promote the English competition’s strength, citing league competitiveness, European results and crowds.

That is a league selling its product as well as celebrating a player. Its comparisons draw on different measures and periods; an individual award cannot, on its own, establish that one domestic competition is superior to every other. Supporters can welcome the arrival of an outstanding footballer without treating the promotional argument as a settled ranking.

The opportunity is more concrete than that. London City now offers fans a place to watch Putellas begin a new chapter, and has attached public commitments about development and ambition to her signing. Those commitments provide a basis for judging what follows.

Putellas has already supplied the performances that earned this recognition. The next responsibility belongs partly to the institutions benefiting from her name: to turn a celebrated arrival into the sporting environment and opportunities they have promised.
